questions.q: Which of the four governance pillars covered in this course does 'workspaces and domains' belong to?
options: Structure
Administration
Security
Trust and lifecycle
questions.explain: Structure covers where content lives and who owns it — workspaces and domains are the core structural units.

questions.q: Does publishing an app automatically expose everything in its source workspace?
options: No — only items explicitly added via the Content tab's 'Add content' are included
Yes — all workspace content becomes visible in the app automatically
Only dashboards are included automatically; reports must be added manually
Apps have no concept of 'content' separate from the workspace
questions.explain: The Content tab's Add content step is how specific items get pulled into the app — publishing doesn't automatically expose everything in the underlying workspace.

questions.q: Where are Power BI workspaces created?
options: In the Power BI service (app.powerbi.com), not in Power BI Desktop
Only in Power BI Desktop, then published to the service
In the Microsoft 365 admin center
Workspaces are created automatically and can't be created manually
questions.explain: Workspaces are created and managed in the Power BI service in a browser. Power BI Desktop can publish into an existing workspace but has no workspace-creation screen.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend 'enabled for specific security groups only' as a safer default for sensitive features like external sharing?
options: It's closed by default and only opens the feature to the people who specifically need it, rather than the whole org
It's the only state that can be changed later without admin permissions
It automatically applies row-level security to the feature
It's required by Microsoft for all tenant settings
questions.explain: Scoping a sensitive setting to specific security groups lets an organization pilot or limit a feature's exposure instead of defaulting to organization-wide access.

questions.q: What is 'workspace sprawl'?
options: Hundreds of flat, unstructured workspaces created ad hoc with no organizing principle
A single workspace that has grown too large in storage size
A tenant setting that limits the number of workspaces a user can create
The automatic archiving of unused workspaces after 90 days
questions.explain: Workspace sprawl describes an unstructured proliferation of workspaces with no naming convention or organizing principle, making discovery and ownership nearly impossible.

questions.q: What has to happen before sensitivity labels appear in Power BI at all?
options: Every semantic model must first be certified
A tenant admin has to enable sensitivity labels for Power BI
Every user must individually request access to labeling
A gateway connection must be configured
questions.explain: Sensitivity labels don't appear in Power BI until a tenant admin enables the feature; once enabled, the organization's existing label taxonomy becomes available on Power BI content.

questions.q: In the Send link dialog, what does the top link-type selector actually control?
options: The file format the report downloads as
Who can use the link at all — people in the org, specific people, or people with existing access
Whether the report refreshes automatically
The sensitivity label applied to the item
questions.explain: The link-type selector is the real access control in the dialog — it determines who can use the link before any individual names are even entered.

questions.q: According to this lesson's checklist, what should happen before calling a semantic model 'production-ready'?
options: Refresh schedule set and history checked, credentials current with a named owner, and owner/sensitivity label set before downstream reports are built
The model must be converted to DirectQuery mode
The model must be published to at least five different workspaces
All tenant settings must be set to 'Enabled for the entire organization'
questions.explain: The checklist covers verifying the refresh schedule is actually working (not just configured), ensuring credentials have a responsible owner, and setting ownership/sensitivity labels before downstream reports proliferate.

questions.q: Before rolling out a new OLS restriction on an existing, widely-used semantic model, what does this lesson recommend?
options: Auditing every report built on the model for references to the object, for the affected role, before publishing
Deleting all existing reports built on the model first
Applying the restriction immediately, since OLS changes are always backward-compatible
Converting the model to DirectQuery mode first
questions.explain: Because hiding an object breaks any reference to it for the affected role, rolling out OLS safely means checking every downstream report for that role's references before publishing the change.

questions.q: What does row-level security (RLS) control?
options: Which workspace a report can be published to
Which rows of data a role's members see, based on a DAX filter
Whether a user can edit a report versus only view it
Which sensitivity label is applied to a dataset
questions.explain: RLS attaches a DAX filter expression to a role, restricting which rows of underlying data that role's members see — two people can view the identical report and see different numbers.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe audit searches as 'saved jobs' rather than one-off queries?
options: Because results are deleted immediately after viewing them once
Because a reviewer can come back later and check a named search's status and results, which matters for investigations spanning several days
Because Power BI requires a new license for every search
Because audit searches can only be run once per year
questions.explain: Audit searches have a name, a status, and are saved, so a reviewer doesn't have to re-run them from scratch — useful for real investigations that unfold over multiple days.

questions.q: Does certification apply only to datasets?
options: Yes, certification is exclusive to datasets and cannot be applied to anything else
No — published apps carry their own Endorse option, and the same certification concept applies there too
No, certification only applies to reports, never datasets
Yes, but only in Power BI Premium
questions.explain: Published apps have their own Endorse option in their settings — the same certification concept (and the same two questions: criteria met, and permission held) extends beyond just datasets.

questions.q: What question does impact analysis answer that lineage view's diagram alone does not?
options: What color scheme the report uses
A counted, listed total of exactly who depends on an item, plus a way to notify them
How much the Power BI Premium capacity costs
Which DAX functions were used in the dataset's measures
questions.explain: Impact analysis gives a real count of impacted child items and workspaces, and adds a direct way to notify every affected contact — capabilities beyond what the lineage diagram alone provides.

questions.q: What is Power BI's usage metrics report?
options: A manually maintained spreadsheet that owners fill in by hand
An auto-generated Power BI report, built once usage metrics is turned on, showing views, viewers, and views-by-user
A setting that automatically deletes unused reports
A certification requirement every dataset must pass before publishing
questions.explain: Turning usage metrics on generates a real, automatically built Power BI report covering views, viewers, and a views-by-user breakdown.

questions.q: Who can set a dataset or report to 'Promoted'?
options: Only the Power BI tenant administrator
Any owner of that item, directly from its settings
Only a user with the Certified permission
Only Microsoft support
questions.explain: Promoting is self-service — any owner can set it from the item's own settings, with no special permission required.

questions.q: Why did the fix start with consolidating workspaces rather than immediately certifying one of the existing reports?
options: Because certification was unavailable to this organization
Because certifying one of three competing, duplicate copies wouldn't fix the underlying problem of three different sources existing at all
Because consolidation is required before anyone can create a workspace
There was no particular reason — the order was arbitrary
questions.explain: Certifying one of three duplicate, inconsistent copies wouldn't address the root cause — the fix had to start by reducing three competing sources down to one owned, governed source.

questions.q: What does a tenant-wide governance status dashboard actually show?
options: Only the names of Power BI reports with no other detail
Domains, workspaces, and item counts, plus coverage signals like how much content has a description or was recently accessed
Only the tenant admin's personal activity
A list of every DAX formula used across the tenant
questions.explain: The governance status view summarizes the whole estate: domain/workspace/item counts alongside coverage measures like descriptions and last-access dates.

questions.q: What is typically true about how teams set up the Test and Production workspaces for a pipeline?
options: They reuse the exact same workspace as Development
They're usually created fresh, specifically for the pipeline, starting with nothing but what the pipeline deploys
They must be created by Microsoft support
They can never be assigned a workspace at all
questions.explain: While Development often points at an existing, actively-worked-in workspace, Test and Production are typically fresh workspaces created specifically for the pipeline.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the fact that each stage is a real workspace matters for governance?
options: It doesn't matter — pipelines have entirely separate security rules
Because everything you already know about governing a workspace (roles, tenant settings, sensitivity labels) still applies to each stage individually
Because it means only one person can ever access all three stages
Because workspaces inside a pipeline can't have sensitivity labels
questions.explain: Since each stage is an ordinary workspace, the roles, tenant settings, and sensitivity labels covered in earlier chapters all still apply — a pipeline doesn't replace that governance, it sits on top of it.

questions.q: What is the purpose of this closing practice lab?
options: To introduce several brand-new Power BI features not covered earlier in the course
To apply every mechanism already covered in this course, yourself, in the order a real governance rollout follows
To replace the need for any of the previous 19 lessons
To test only Chapter 4's content in isolation
questions.explain: The lab is explicitly a structured walk-through reusing this course's existing concepts, applied hands-on in a realistic rollout order, rather than new material.
